chapters.title: The Super Salesperson's Secret Weapon
chapters.summary: Car buyers' journeys are long with many touchpoints. Look at online comparison volume and semantics to see your real rivals and the appeals to strengthen.

chapters.title: From Black Swans to Gray Rhinos: The Adaptability Quotient Every Brand Needs
chapters.summary: Use a crisis-relevance and market-demand matrix to find where you stand, then turn crisis into opportunity with the five A.R.I.S.E. adaptability quotients.

chapters.title: Data-Driven Marketing Through the Lens of COVID-19
chapters.summary: Walled gardens and dying cookies leave marketers seeing fragments. Use different data sources at each journey stage, then link them with data fusion.

chapters.title: Using Salesforce to Unify Brand Data, Improve Customer Experience, and Drive Growth
chapters.summary: Before adopting martech, set a customer relationship blueprint, then use five keys to connect everything from first-party data to reporting.

chapters.title: Not Just a Better World but Client Results: Full-Funnel Creative That Proves Integrated Creative and Media
chapters.summary: Use the funnel as a shared language to unite creative and performance: find the stuck layer, test on a small budget, then scale up.

chapters.title: Outpacing Rivals in Digital: The New Era of the “Search 4V” Is Here
chapters.summary: Behind every search is a real person. Build organic search across four types: voice, image, vertical, and universal.

chapters.title: How Media Performance Connects to Sales Targets
chapters.summary: Split goals into business, market, and communication layers, find the most valuable consumers, then use econometric models to estimate media's sales impact.

chapters.title: Disruptive Innovation in Precision Marketing
chapters.summary: With third-party cookies gone, rebuild precision marketing with contextual targeting, a first-party CDP, and machine-learning auto-optimization.

chapters.title: AI X Creativity
chapters.summary: AI can churn out banners in seconds and predict performance; creatives' value shifts to refinement, strategy, and full-funnel creative.

chapters.title: Marketing Measurement Decoded
chapters.summary: Data isn't truth. Martech favors short-term measurable metrics, so weigh data quality and quantity, plus human judgment and surveys. The main job cites its Adidas case.

chapters.title: Tech-Empowered: The Big Health Wave Arrives
chapters.summary: Wearables and AI shift health toward prevention and personalization. Taiwan gains three markets: health data services, mental health, and community habit building.

chapters.title: Report on Japan's Health Industry
chapters.by: Dentsu Taiwan, Dentsu Kuohua, Isobar Taiwan
chapters.summary: Japan shifted focus from average to healthy life expectancy; companies turn social issues into business via functional foods, channel shifts, and senior services.

chapters.title: Taiwan's Health, Seen Through Data
chapters.summary: Taiwanese value health but don't prioritize spending on it. Knowing beats doing; they prefer low-barrier options and rely on channels where someone explains.

chapters.title: Supplements and OTC Drugs: Breaking Down Market Dynamics
chapters.summary: Broad health supplements and OTC drugs outgrow regular FMCG; the keys are diverse product formats and differentiated channel execution.

chapters.title: Conclusion: Get Ahead of the Curve with Strategies to Ride the Big Health Wave
chapters.summary: Health is going personalized, smart, and prevention-first. Companies need cross-industry partners, health data, and service design to upgrade products.

chapters.title: Media Genesis: Who Gets on the Ark?
chapters.summary: Audiences shift from aimless browsing to purposeful on-demand; social and search are the gateways. To be seen, brands must make content people need.

chapters.title: An Unbalanced Media Ecosystem
chapters.summary: Self-media upended the balance of media, audiences, and advertisers. Hard sells fail, subscriptions and echo chambers rise; marketers need new roles and focus.

chapters.title: The Death of Third-Party Cookie Marketing
chapters.summary: Chrome phasing out third-party cookies hits tracking, audiences, and retargeting; advertisers must shift to building first-party data and content.

npcs.name: Asst. Mgr. Ko
npcs.title: Asst. Marketing Mgr, No-Look Reverse
lines: Everyone online is talking about our car, but nobody comes in for a test drive.
The demo car sits at City Hall Station. What people touch most is the side mirror.
The boss says being loudest online means we win. I'm not so sure.

npcs.name: Ah-Che
npcs.title: Copywriter, Second Year
lines: AI made 300 overnight. I haven't finished looking at even one.
Quick question: who came up with the name “Never Burn Out”?
AI scored my headline a 60. I'm genuinely hurt.

npcs.name: Ms. Chou
npcs.title: Founder, Walk & Earn Health App
lines: We want seniors walking a thousand more steps a day, starting at the general store.
Data matters, but grandparents matter more than data.
Lots of downloads. Very few people still walking by week two.

npcs.name: Pharmacist Cheng
npcs.title: Convenience Store Pharmacist
lines: The first thing every customer asks: does this stuff actually work?
However many ads they see, they still end up at my counter asking me.
More supplements isn't better. It depends on what you're missing.

missions.title: Most Buzz, Fewest Test Drives
missions.brief: Car brand “No-Look Reverse” leads online buzz yet trails in test-drive bookings. Asst. Mgr. Ko waits by the City Hall Station demo car; his boss wants more buzz.

lines.text: {role}, look at this report. Our online buzz is number one in our class.
But test drives are near the bottom. Boss says buzz isn't enough; get more car reviewers.
When people online mention you, who do they compare you to?
We always assumed the two German brands. But nobody actually puts us in their comparisons.
Folks at the demo car keep asking if a stroller fits in back. Our ads all talk horsepower.

steps.prompt: Asst. Mgr. Ko pitches next quarter's plan next week. What do you suggest?

options.text: Do what the boss says: get five car reviewers to do unboxings and push the buzz even higher.
options.feedback: Each unboxing video beats the last, and buzz breaks records again. Test-drive bookings tick up a few, mostly reviewers' fans coming to take photos.
options.insight: The analysis in “The Super Salesperson's Secret Weapon” found a brand with the most mentions but the fewest comparisons; the cars consumers compare you to are your real rivals.

options.text: Check comparison volume: on comparison sites, who are we lined up against, and on which specs?
options.feedback: Ah-Kai pulls three months of comparison data: the car most often compared isn't German, it's a domestic SUV. Asst. Mgr. Ko's competitor deck gets rebuilt from scratch.
options.insight: The book finds Mercedes-Benz's top rival is itself, at 30% of its model comparisons; track mentions and comparison volume together, and how one converts into the other.

options.text: Use buyer psychology: space, parking, safety. Shift the ads from horsepower to “fits a stroller.”
options.feedback: The new creative runs a week at City Hall Station, and people start bringing strollers to test the fit. Within a month, test-drive bookings climb to mid-pack.
options.insight: Drawing on “Automotive Psychology,” the book lays out seven psychological decision factors and scores each car's attributes from 178 hardware specs, scientifically finding the appeals a brand should strengthen.

inline.q: Per “The Super Salesperson's Secret Weapon,” at least how many information channels do car buyers use online when deciding?
inline.explain: Buyers' decisions take about 3 months, or 90 days, gathering info online from at least 24 different channels and browsing 10 or more models.

card.title: Compared Means Competing
card.text: Everyone talking about you isn't everyone wanting to buy you. First, find whose comparison chart you're in.

missions.title: A Week of Rain, Higher Fees
missions.brief: A week of plum rains halved the crowds on Linginger Street, and the delivery app raised its cut again. Ah-Cheng wants to hike prices; the next stall wants to team up.

lines.text: {role}, a week of rain, half the customers, and the delivery app wants a bigger cut.
They take over 30% of every chicken cutlet. If I don't raise prices, I'm working for free.
Are the stalls next door in the same spot?
The whole street is. The oyster omelet guy says we should just hire our own riders.
My daughter says post memes riding the news. You're in advertising. What do you think?

steps.prompt: How does Ah-Cheng get through this rainy season?

options.text: Team up with the street on night-market riders: order from several stalls on LINE, one trip home.
options.feedback: Week one has just two riders, and cutlets and oyster omelets bounce on one scooter until cold. By week three, with insulated boxes and a third rider, orders hold steady.
options.insight: In “From Black Swans to Gray Rhinos,” Carat cites Taiwan night markets launching their own delivery riders: combined orders across stalls beat platform fees and solve two pain points, going out and waiting in line.

options.text: Ride the news: post a “Rainy-Day Chicken Rescue Squad” meme while the downpour is trending.
options.feedback: The meme gets shared thousands of times, and a short line forms the day the rain stops. One comment: places are still cleaning up floods and you're selling chicken?
options.insight: Relevance in A.R.I.S.E. means riding an issue to win mindshare; the book cites Sunflower's lutein ad pitted against bananas. Beyond the book: where riding an issue becomes exploiting it is your call.

options.text: Offer small rainy-day combos at unchanged prices, so ordering less from home still feels worth it.
options.feedback: A small cutlet plus black tea as a rainy-day combo sells out on day one. Ah-Cheng says margins are a bit thinner, but his regulars stuck around.
options.insight: One of the book's three key mindsets is “opportunity survives, but demand changes”; answering new needs with agility and innovation weathers a crisis better than clinging to old ways.

inline.q: What does “From Black Swans to Gray Rhinos” advise brands in markets where demand surges during a crisis?
options: Raise prices while demand is high
Hold prices so you don't look like a profiteer
inline.explain: The book advises against raising prices in surging markets, so consumers don't feel you're profiting from disaster.
inline.source: From Black Swans to Gray Rhinos: The Adaptability Quotient Every Brand Needs

card.title: Needs Change, Opportunity Stays
card.text: When crisis hits, first ask what your customers need now, not how much you can raise prices.

missions.title: The Retargeting List Vanished
missions.brief: Browsers keep blocking third-party cookies, and Manager Chen's sleep supplement retargeting list is down to 20%. At Lanshan Plaza she asks who her ads can still find.

lines.text: {role}, our retargeting list for the new sleep aid is just 20% of last year's.
People who visited our site kept seeing us. Now it's like tossing ads into the sea.
Cookie blocking is killing cross-site tracking. But your members and LINE friends remain.
When sleep-aid buyers can't sleep, what are they looking at?
I wish I knew. People scrolling at 2 AM sure aren't looking at supplements.

steps.prompt: How should you replan the second-half digital budget?

options.text: Go contextual: let the system read articles and place ads next to ones on insomnia and stress.
options.feedback: Ads run beside “Waking up at night?” and out-click old retargeting. Once, one lands by a piece on sleeping-pill side effects, and you add exclusion terms overnight.
options.insight: Amnet's “Disruptive Innovation in Precision Marketing” says that with cookies gone, NLP enables contextual targeting, turning unstructured articles into structured tags and serving by content, not individual tracking.

options.text: Build a first-party data platform: merge members, LINE, and e-com orders, then let ML optimize.
options.feedback: Integration takes four months; Ah-Kai says he matches fields in his dreams. After launch, media costs drop a lot, but this quarter's sales report looks ugly.
options.insight: The book says ads served by machine learning on owned traffic unified in a CDP cut CPA by over 50% and CPC by over 60% on average, and free marketers from reports.

options.text: Split the journey: survey and social data for awareness, your own members for purchase.
options.feedback: You find sleepless people mostly listen to podcasts at night, so awareness budget moves to audio; purchase-stage pushes go only to LINE friends. Less spend, sales hold.
options.insight: Amplifi says walled gardens show marketers only fragments, so use different data sources at each journey stage and link them with data fusion; but fusion only works with respondent-level data.

inline.q: “Data-Driven Marketing Through the Lens of COVID-19” says Dentsu Japan's 2005 AISAS model was revised in 2017 into what?
inline.explain: Dentsu Japan proposed AISAS in 2005 and revised it into Dual AISAS in 2017 to describe more complex customer journeys.
inline.source: Data-Driven Marketing Through the Lens of COVID-19

card.title: Can't Track People? Read Context
card.text: Tracking individuals is harder now; brands that know people's context and what they read can still find them.

missions.title: AI Made 300 Overnight
missions.brief: Players keep leaving the mobile game “Never Burn Out.” Overnight, AI generated 300 ad images and gave each a predicted score. Ah-Che, your junior, asks: run them all?

lines.text: {role}, AI made 300 “Never Burn Out” banners overnight.
Each has a predicted CTR. Mine scored 60 and ranked 240th.
Does the client want new players, or to bring old ones back?
Both. It's been out two years. Everyone knows it; they just don't want to open it again.
Director Lin wants a direction by ten. I'm getting coffee first. I need it.

steps.prompt: What direction do you give these 300 by ten?

options.text: Run them all, let the system go for a week, and let CTR weed them out.
options.feedback: Week one's top CTR is a “Free 10x Pull” banner, and downloads jump. Week two falls back to baseline; most returning players pull and leave.
options.insight: Dentsu Kuohua's “AI X Creativity” presents ADAM, which makes a banner every five seconds; a prediction engine then estimates CTR and ranks them by brand or direct-response goals.

options.text: AI makes the volume; people pick the top ten to polish and guard the brand's voice.
options.feedback: You and Ah-Che revise till 11:30, keep four of the top ten, and add two headlines he wrote by hand. Results beat average; the client says it finally feels like them.
options.insight: The book quotes a Dentsu Japan leader: people will never be replaced by AI. AI handles mass output, and creatives' time shifts to refinement and strategy.

options.text: Skip the images: find where players drop in the funnel, then test the best appeal on a small budget.
options.feedback: Interviews show old players want to return, but their friends left. You switch to “Bring a friend back, both get rewards,” test small before scaling, and returns climb.
options.insight: Dentsu Taiwan's full-funnel creative finds the stuck layer first; for a mobile game, it tests the strongest “appeal × character” combo on a small budget, then scales to outdoor and TV.

inline.q: In the “ad co-creation” process in “AI X Creativity,” what is the last step after AI produces banners?
options: Client picks one and it goes live
Media platform auto-reviews and serves it
Prediction engine picks the version alone
inline.explain: The book says that after AI produces banners, creatives refine and confirm them to finish the design; that's the new way of “ad co-creation.”

card.title: Volume to AI, Judgment to People
card.text: AI makes 300 a night, but people still judge which funnel layer is broken and which one fits the brand.

missions.title: Breakfast Near Me? Not Us
missions.brief: Auntie Hsiu-chin's granddaughter asked her phone for “breakfast near me” and got only chains. This breakfast shop has run for twenty years, yet online it barely exists.

lines.text: {role}, my granddaughter asked her phone for “breakfast near me.” We didn't show up.
All chains popped up, plus one that only opened last month.
Is our menu or any photos of the shop online?
Customers posted some. The egg crepes look like rags. And it lists us closed Mondays.
The place next door says they bought ads. Should I buy some too?

steps.prompt: Auntie Hsiu-chin will only spend a little each month. Your advice?

options.text: Buy map and keyword ads so “breakfast near me” finds the shop first.
options.feedback: The ads go live and new customers really do come. Every month Auntie Hsiu-chin frowns at the bill and asks if she has to keep paying forever.
options.insight: iProspect says integrating SEO and SEM raises search quality scores, letting paid search win better spots at lower CPC; paid and organic search need tending together.

options.text: Write the shop info as Q&A: opening hours, vegetarian options, preorders. Add captions to photos.
options.feedback: You and Auntie Hsiu-chin's granddaughter spend a weekend fixing hours and writing twelve Q&As. Two weeks on, ask a phone for “breakfast open at 6 AM” and they're first.
options.insight: “Search 4V” says 27% of people worldwide regularly use voice search and voice queries lean toward questions, so use FAQ structure; images need good alt text so search engines can read them.

options.text: Shoot a 15-second griddle clip each morning: flipping crepes, regulars saying hi. Post on schedule.
options.feedback: Auntie Hsiu-chin starts out shy, but clip five, where she fumbles a crepe flip, gets the most views. One comment says it reminds them of the shop on their own corner.
options.insight: Carat's “Media Genesis” says people have shifted from aimless browsing to purposeful on-demand, with social and search as the two gateways; the only way to be searchable and crawlable is content people need.

inline.q: What phrase does “Media Genesis” use for brands' future battle for visibility in media?
options: Buy it with budget, borrow it without
Follow trends when there are some, make them when there aren't
Searchable with a purpose, crawlable without one
Keep members when you have them, win them back when you don't
inline.explain: The book says brands' future media war is a visibility war: searchable when people have a purpose (search visibility), crawlable when they don't.
inline.source: Media Genesis: Who Gets on the Ark?

card.title: Be Findable First
card.text: People no longer wander aimlessly; they ask. Brands must be searchable the moment they ask.

missions.title: Contract Demands 10% Growth
missions.brief: Over stir-fry, Manager Hsu of a cleaning brand says next year's contract needs “ads drive 10% sales growth,” or fees get docked. Her boss loves favorability reports.

lines.text: {role}, bad news: next year's contract demands 10% sales growth, or fees get cut.
My boss says, aren't you great with data? Then guarantee it with data.
Is that 10% from new customers, or old ones buying more?
…I don't know either. I just know he loves reading that monthly favorability report.
10% growth? If my stir-fry joint grew 10%, I'd go tour the whole island.

steps.prompt: You have to answer on the contract terms tomorrow. Your advice?

options.text: Accept, but first run an econometric model on sales data to split out price, channel, and media.
options.feedback: After three weeks of modeling, media can carry about four points; distribution and price do the rest. Manager Hsu's chart sways her boss, and the clause becomes itemized.
options.insight: Vizeum's “How Media Performance Connects to Sales Targets” uses the econometric tool Velocity with client sales data to estimate each medium's contribution to sales.

options.text: Don't promise sales: split goals into business, market, and communication tiers with metrics we own.
options.feedback: Manager Hsu first thinks you're dodging, but when you get to “whose penetration has to grow,” she grabs a pen. The contract ends up with three layers of metrics.
options.insight: Using 10% sales growth as its example, the book argues for splitting it into business, market, and communication goals, finding the most valuable consumers, then deciding media and messaging.

options.text: Lean on favorability and brand-lift reports next year. The boss loves them; the numbers look good.
options.feedback: Reports improve every quarter and the boss is pleased. At year-end, finance finds sales flat; only then do they see the reports and the register tell different stories.
options.insight: dentsu X's “Marketing Measurement Decoded” warns data isn't truth: brand-lift studies require random, uncontaminated test and control groups, and over-optimizing short-term metrics erodes long-term value.

inline.q: “Marketing Measurement Decoded” says there were about 150 martech companies in 2011. How many were there by 2019?
inline.explain: Martech companies numbered about 150 in 2011 and topped 7,000 by 2019; growth has only recently slowed.

card.title: Split It to Carry It
card.text: 10% sales growth isn't one number but several layers of goals; split them up to see which layer ads can carry.

missions.title: A Thousand Steps at the Store
missions.brief: A health app wants a step kiosk at the Sisi South Village general store: seniors trade steps for points while it collects health data. Ama sits at the door, unconvinced.

lines.text: {role}, we want a kiosk at the general store. Seniors tap a band daily for points.
Steps, sleep, heart rate all come in. Later we can give personalized health advice.
I walk to the market every day. That's ten thousand steps already. Why tap some band?
Who gets to see this data later? Who keeps it safe?
Us, partner clinics, maybe insurers… we're still working that out.

steps.prompt: Ms. Chou meets the borough chief next week. What should she do first?

options.text: Cross-industry: store, borough chief, clinic. Steps earn store points; monthly blood pressure check.
options.feedback: Forty seniors join in month one; Ama gets dragged in too, “for the soy sauce points.” Data custody takes Ms. Chou three talks with the clinic to write into the contract.
options.insight: The conclusion, “Get Ahead of the Curve,” raises three key ideas: cross-industry partnership, owning the value of health data, and upgrading products with service design. Beyond the book: settle first who owns and secures health data.

options.text: Personalize first: each senior sees their own steps and sleep tips; data shared only with consent.
options.feedback: The consent form takes two tries. The first has tiny print; one old lady says she'll go ask her grandson. Version two is read aloud, and sign-ups finally pick up.
options.insight: “Tech-Empowered: The Big Health Wave Arrives” notes wearables ship over 200M units a year, but data is just the warm-up; what makes people healthier is the analysis and personalized service after.

options.text: No data yet. A walking group at the store every Wednesday afternoon makes walking a reason to meet.
options.feedback: Only six come the first time; by week four it's thirty, all buying soda at the store afterward. App downloads barely move, but those who stay show up every week.
options.insight: The book names three potential markets in Taiwan, one being community-driven habit building; Sports Administration data shows only 34% exercise regularly. The hard part is keeping people at it.

inline.q: What three health-industry trends does “Conclusion: Get Ahead of the Curve with Strategies to Ride the Big Health Wave” name?
inline.explain: The conclusion centers on three trends, personalized, smart, and prevention over cure, and draws on Japan's experience to propose strategies.
inline.source: Conclusion: Get Ahead of the Curve with Strategies to Ride the Big Health Wave

card.title: People Before Data
card.text: Collecting health data isn't hard. Getting people to keep walking daily, and trust you with their data, is.

missions.title: Does This Stuff Work?
missions.brief: Lutein brand “No More Dry Eyes” wants to go all-in on digital ads. Pharmacist Cheng at the Corner Convenience Store says customers still end up at her counter asking.

lines.text: {role}, the “No More Dry Eyes” rep says this year's budget all goes to online ads.
But after the ads, customers still come ask me: does this stuff actually work?
What do you usually tell them?
First I ask their daily screen hours, then what else they take. Some take five at once.
Young people do ask if there's a drink version. They say capsules are hard to swallow.

steps.prompt: How should the brand split next quarter's budget?

options.text: Go with the rep: mostly digital ads, targeting people with long screen time.
options.feedback: Reach looks great and searches rise. More people ask at pharmacy counters, but no one trained pharmacists on this product, so some leave after asking.
options.insight: “Taiwan's Health, Seen Through Data” notes digital channels matter more for health info every year, and by 2019 were on par with TV.

options.text: Put 30% into pharmacist training and counter info cards so the front line knows what to say.
options.feedback: You run small sessions at thirty pharmacies and come home hoarse nightly. Two months on, Pharmacist Cheng says she now recommends it; she can explain how it's different.
options.insight: Nielsen's analysis finds that at pharmacies, the key to purchase isn't visibility but the pharmacist's recommendation; at personal-care stores, shoppers care most about finding the product easily.

options.text: Change the format: launch a lutein drink and 7-day packs so young people can try it.
options.feedback: Factory scheduling delays the new packs a month. Once the lutein drink hits convenience store fridges, young office workers rebuy it far more than capsules.
options.insight: Nielsen finds broad health growth comes from diverse product formats; lutein drinks only entered the market in 2016, gained share three years running, and grew fastest of any segment.

inline.q: “Taiwan's Health, Seen Through Data” estimates the 2019 supplement market topped NT$145B. How much did it grow over ten years?
inline.explain: The book estimates the 2019 supplement market topped NT$145B, up 82% over ten years, with 75% penetration.

card.title: The Last Mile Is the Counter
card.text: Health matters but isn't urgent spending; what gets people to pay is often one explanation at the counter.

missions.title: Healthy Years at the Temple
missions.brief: Skincare brand “Wrinkles Off Duty” wants a booth at the Fude St. Earth God Shrine's blessing festival. Temple Uncle says seniors come in droves, but no sales pitches.

lines.text: Young one, a skincare brand wants a blessing festival booth with free samples for seniors.
I'm not against it. But last time a mattress seller came, one old lady bought three.
What do the seniors who come to pray worry about most?
Weak legs, bad sleep, fear of falling. Some say they're old and avoid the mirror.
I'm fine. I put on lipstick every day. It cheers me up, and I walk stronger too.

steps.prompt: How do you suggest the brand join the blessing festival?

options.text: Set up a booth with samples: scan to join as a member for 10% off. Works best when it's crowded.
options.feedback: A long line forms and 300 members sign up in a day. The next week Temple Uncle calls: someone's son came to the temple asking who signed his dad up.
options.insight: Beyond the book: Japan's Foods with Function Claims system, launched in 2015, has loose certification and fast launches and is the fastest-growing category; but the book's Japanese firms more often turn aging into long-term services.

options.text: Run a makeup and grooming class for seniors, taught by beauty advisors, not salespeople.
options.feedback: Twenty grandmas come to the first class; one says she hasn't drawn her brows in forty years. They end with a group photo out front; the brand gives each just a lip balm.
options.insight: “Report on Japan's Health Industry” cites Shiseido: in 2013 it proposed “cosmetic therapy” as a new way to slow aging in an aging society, opening beauty classes and training caregivers.

options.text: Do it Japan's way: free body-fat and grip tests, retested quarterly at the temple to track change.
options.feedback: After the first test, many seniors take their slips to Temple Uncle to ask what the numbers mean. At the next quarter's retest, half come back, bringing neighbors.
options.insight: The book cites TANITA: it launched the world's first body-fat scale in 1992, then expanded from measurement to healthy meals and cafeterias. Japan has shifted from average to healthy life expectancy.

inline.q: Per “Report on Japan's Health Industry,” how many years apart are average and healthy life expectancy for older Japanese?
inline.explain: For older Japanese, average and healthy life expectancy differ by about 10 years; attention has shifted from how long people live to how long they stay healthy.

card.title: Live Long, Live Well
card.text: The senior market doesn't need more sales pitches; it needs services that make the healthy years last longer.

missions.title: The Delivery Rider's Channel
missions.brief: Delivery rider Ah-Chieh's “Rider's Daily” channel has 80K subs; helmet brand “Breathe Easy” wants him for live commerce. At Rainbow Riverside he asks: take it or not?

lines.text: {role}, “Breathe Easy” wants a helmet livestream. One show outpays a week of runs.
But my viewers are all riders. They hate sponsored posts. The comments will explode.
Did the brand mention any other approach?
They're thinking of starting their own channel, but their page gets ten likes a post.
And a rider group chat says, why don't we all design a helmet that doesn't get stuffy?

steps.prompt: What would you suggest the brand do?

options.text: Have Ah-Chieh do live commerce, testing it for three hours in the rain. Add shows if it sells.
options.feedback: The livestream sells 800 helmets; comments split, haters vs. fans. The brand, thrilled, books three more influencers, but none of those viewers are the brand's own.
options.insight: “An Unbalanced Media Ecosystem” cites a survey: global influencer budgets hit US$6.5B in 2019, and 63% of companies planned to spend more in 2020. Beyond the book: influencers persuade, but one-off exposure rarely builds the brand's own assets.

options.text: The brand runs its own channel, posting rider lifestyle content every week, no rush to sell.
options.feedback: Subs look grim for three months; the brand nearly quits. In month four, “My Head After 10 Hours in a Summer Helmet” blows up; now people wait for each week's video.
options.insight: One new focus the book lists for marketers is regular, everyday brand content: going from four campaigns a year to 150 social posts.

options.text: Co-create with riders: collect design ideas in the group chat, then crowdfund a new model.
options.feedback: The group argues for two months, 300 messages on vents alone. The crowdfund hits its goal in the first hour; Ah-Chieh says it's the first helmet he's wanted to recommend.
options.insight: The book mentions a Taiwanese creator's crowdfunding campaign that drew 26,980 backers in one day; self-media and social upended the old balance among media, audiences, and advertisers.

inline.q: “An Unbalanced Media Ecosystem” says that when marketing goes from four campaigns a year to 150 posts, what do brands always lack?
inline.explain: The book says brands always lack content; finding a content angle and long-term content partners is the first step into consumers' lives.

card.title: Borrowed Audiences Leave
card.text: Influencers can sell for you for a night; only an audience you grow yourself waits for your next video.
